name: Tanning gummies / supplements
lead: Tanning gummies and tanning pills are oral products sold to give skin a deeper, tan-looking colour without sun or sunbeds. Depending on the product they contain carotenoid pigments such as beta-carotene, astaxanthin or (in older pills) canthaxanthin, or the amino acid L-tyrosine, which is marketed as a building block for melanin.[3][4][6] People take them as a swallowed alternative to sunless tanning lotions and sprays, aiming for an even, all-over bronze that needs no application and no UV exposure.[1][3]

The pigment-based products work by colouring the skin from within. Carotenoids are the orange, yellow and red pigments of carrots, tomatoes and some seafood; taken in large amounts for several weeks they accumulate in the outer skin layers and in the fat beneath, giving a golden-orange tint known medically as carotenosis.[8] Canthaxanthin deposits in the subcutaneous fat and gives a golden-orange shade.[2] Because the colour comes from the pigment itself, it does not involve melanin, and it fades over weeks to months after intake stops.[8]

Regulators and medical groups have commented on these products for decades. The US FDA has approved no tanning pills, and treats canthaxanthin tanning products as adulterated cosmetics; the American Cancer Society and dermatologists quoted in the press note that the pills give no protection from UV light.[2][3][6] No published clinical trial has tested a modern tanning gummy for cosmetic outcomes.

chain: Swallow a carotenoid pigment (beta-carotene or canthaxanthin)
Pigment is stored in skin and the fat layer beneath it
Skin takes on a golden-orange, tan-like colour
angle.text: The colour change comes from the pigment accumulating in the body, so the skin can look warmer and more bronzed without UV exposure. The shade is typically golden-orange rather than the brown produced by melanin, and it builds up over weeks of regular intake and fades slowly.

paras: Oral tanners are sold as gummies, chews, tablets and capsules, often in flavoured, supplement-style packaging. Their ingredient lists fall into two broad groups. The first is carotenoid pigments: beta-carotene, which the body also converts to vitamin A, lycopene from tomatoes, astaxanthin and, in older pills, canthaxanthin, a keto-carotenoid used as a food and feed colourant.[2][4][9] The second is tanning-accelerator ingredients, usually the amino acid tyrosine, which is marketed as supporting the body's own melanin production.[1][7]

The Cleveland Clinic describes the carotenoid pills as settling in the upper skin layers and producing an orange tint in some people rather than a true tan, with colour tending to collect on thicker skin such as palms and soles.[4] The American Cancer Society lists tanning gummies containing carotenoids such as beta-carotene as marketed to tint skin from the inside out.[3]

Excess carotene in the blood and skin produces a harmless yellow-orange tint called carotenosis, carotenaemia or carotenoderma.[8][9] Reference sources say signs typically appear after about 4 to 7 weeks of high intake, and that the colour is most visible in light-skinned people, collecting at the palms, soles, knees and the folds beside the nose.[8] It spares the whites of the eyes, which is how it is told apart from jaundice, and it is reversible: skin colour returns to normal after intake stops, which can take several months.[8]

Wikipedia's carotenoid pages report that carotenoid pigments are stored mainly in body fat.[9] Canthaxanthin tanning pills used far larger amounts than the quantities used to colour foods, and deposit in the fat layer under the skin.[2][4]

Canthaxanthin pills were sold as products that simulate a tan, with the pigment depositing in the subcutaneous fat and giving the skin a golden-orange hue.[2] In the late 1980s, reversible crystal-like deposits in the retina were reported in people who had taken very high amounts from tanning pills; they disappeared after stopping and the affected people recovered.[2] A 2003 FDA publication linked tanning pills to canthaxanthin retinopathy, liver injury and hives, citing the American Academy of Dermatology.[2] A 2011 study by Hueber and colleagues concluded that the retinal deposits were reversible and caused no lasting morphological change.[2]

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives set an acceptable daily intake for canthaxanthin as a food colour of 0.03 mg per kg of body weight in 1995; the EU Scientific Committee for Food accepted it in 1997 and EFSA reconfirmed it in 2010. Canthaxanthin is an approved food colour (E161g) in the US and EU but not in Australia or New Zealand.[2] These figures concern use as a food additive, not tanning.

Modern tanning gummies generally use these carotenoids rather than canthaxanthin. The American Cancer Society notes they are not FDA-approved for tanning and not regulated as such, and that high doses raise the chance of harmful effects including liver toxicity.[3] Wikipedia reports that chronic high-dose synthetic beta-carotene supplements have been linked to higher lung cancer rates in smokers, and that a 2013 meta-analysis associated intakes of at least 9.6 mg a day with a 6 percent increase in all-cause mortality; medical authorities generally suggest getting beta-carotene from food.[9]
The Cleveland Clinic adds that, because supplements are less tightly regulated than drugs, a product may contain different amounts of ingredients than the label states.[4]

A second product family appeals to the idea that a swallowed amino acid can feed melanin synthesis. L-tyrosine is a precursor of melanin, which the body makes with the enzyme tyrosinase, and TikTok users have promoted tyrosine supplements as a way to tan.[7] Wikipedia describes tanning accelerators, lotions or pills usually containing tyrosine, as claiming to speed tanning when combined with UV exposure, and reports that no scientific data support the claims.[1]

Dermatologists quoted by NewBeauty include Dr. Jacquiline Habashy, who called the idea "no more than a TikTok trend" and said no studies support oral tyrosine producing a tan, and Dr. Deborah Longwill, who said there is no scientific proof it produces a tan.[7] The Fox News dermatologists note that L-tyrosine may interact with certain medications and may worsen hyperthyroidism.[6]

The FDA has approved no tanning pills. In June 2004 it sent warning letters to two firms marketing canthaxanthin capsules, American Sports Nutrition of Fargo, North Dakota, and RPM Total Vitality of Yorba Linda, California; the agency said claims of protection against sunburn, genetic damage and skin cancer were drug claims, and that tanning claims made the product an adulterated cosmetic.[5] Wikipedia notes that the agency has issued later warnings citing an unsafe colour additive, and that canthaxanthin is approved as a food colour but not as a tanning agent.[1][2]
The American Cancer Society states that tanning pills and gummies are not FDA-approved and sit outside the agency's oversight.[3]

Dermatologists and the American Cancer Society generally group oral tanners with other sunless approaches. The most widely used is topical dihydroxyacetone (DHA), which the FDA approves for external use and which reacts with proteins in the outer skin layer to give a temporary darker colour that fades within days.[1][3] DHA's tanning effect was reported by Eva Wittgenstein at Cincinnati Children's Hospital in the 1950s; Man-Tan (1959) and Coppertone's QT (1960) were early consumer products whose orange tone hurt their reputation.[1]

Melanotan injections and nasal sprays are a different category: they are marketed with reference to afamelanotide, are not approved for tanning, and have been the subject of health-agency warnings since 2007.[1][3] They are not oral tanning pills and are not covered by the gummy category.

Oral tanners are discussed in appearance communities as one of several routes to a bronzed look, alongside sunless lotions, sprays and sunbeds. The appeal is that the colour is even, needs no application and leaves no streaks. Reports of orange tinting, especially on palms and in skin folds, are a recurring theme in coverage of carotenoid products.[4][8]

Press coverage, including Fox News in 2024 and NewBeauty, followed social-media interest in tanning pills, tyrosine and related trends, quoting dermatologists who stressed that the products do not protect against UV and who questioned whether tyrosine can produce a tan.[6][7] Dr. Alexis Young of Hackensack University Medical Center was quoted in Fox News as saying the risks for skin cancer and liver damage outweigh any perceived benefits.[6] Dermatologist Dr. Amy Kassouf is quoted by the Cleveland Clinic as stating that tanning pills do not work well and are not worth the potential danger.[4]

timeline.event: Eva Wittgenstein reports the skin-staining effect of DHA, leading to sunless tanners.[1]
Man-Tan, the first commercial DHA self-tanner, launches; Coppertone QT follows in 1960.[1]
Reversible retinal crystal deposits reported in some people taking very high amounts of canthaxanthin from tanning pills.[2]
JECFA sets an acceptable daily intake for canthaxanthin as a food colour.[2]
An FDA publication links tanning pills to canthaxanthin retinopathy, liver injury and hives.[2]
FDA warning letters (24 and 29 June) to two firms marketing canthaxanthin capsules as tanning pills.[5]
FDA warning letter (5 April) to a firm marketing a canthaxanthin product, describing such products as adulterated cosmetics.[2]
Health agencies begin warning against melanotan tanning products.[1]
Hueber and colleagues report reversible retinal deposits without lasting structural change.[2]
Press coverage of social-media tanning-pill trends quotes dermatologists on risks.[6]

lore.intro: Oral tanners are discussed on social media and in appearance communities as a no-UV route to a tan, with both pigment (carotenoid) and melanin-support (tyrosine) products promoted.[6][7]

claims.claim: Tanning gummies give a natural-looking tan from the inside out
claims.believers: Marketing for the gummies describes colour that tints skin from the inside out, with no application or streaks.[3]
claims.experts: The pigment is a carotenoid that tints skin golden-orange rather than producing melanin, and collects on palms and soles; dermatologists say the colour can look unnatural.[4][8]

claims.believers: TikTok users say tyrosine, a melanin precursor, boosts the body's own pigment and helps tanning.[7]
claims.experts: Dermatologists quoted in the press say no studies support oral tyrosine producing a tan, and Wikipedia says no scientific data support tyrosine tanning accelerators.[1][7]

claims.claim: A pill tan also protects the skin from burning
claims.believers: Some marketers have claimed protection against sunburn and skin damage; the FDA treated such claims for canthaxanthin capsules as drug claims in 2004.[5]
claims.experts: The American Cancer Society states that tanning pills give no UV protection, and dermatologists warn that darker-looking skin may lead people to feel falsely safe in the sun.[3][6]

claims.claim: Because the ingredients are from food, the pills are harmless
claims.believers: Users note that beta-carotene and lycopene occur in vegetables and tomatoes.[4]
claims.experts: The American Cancer Society cites liver toxicity at high doses, and Wikipedia reports beta-carotene supplements are linked to higher lung cancer rates in smokers; canthaxanthin tanning doses have caused reversible retinal deposits.[2][3][9]

claims.claim: The orange colour is only temporary
claims.believers: Users say the tint fades after stopping the product.[8]
claims.experts: Carotenosis is described as benign and reversible, but resolution can take several months.[8]

card.summary: Carotenoid chews and pills sold to deepen a tan; no tanning approval and past retinal and liver concerns.
card.note: FDA has warned against tanning pills.

quick.overview:
These are chews or pills, often with carotenoids, marketed to make skin look tanner.

No tanning pill is FDA-approved, and no trial supports the gummy format.
quick.mechanism: Carotenoids such as canthaxanthin deposit in fat under the skin and tint it golden-orange.[2]
quick.risks: High-dose canthaxanthin has been linked to retinal deposits, liver injury and hives;[2] beta-carotene to lung cancer in smokers at high doses.[1]
